1: This is a technical deep dive from the Federal Modernization Workbook's Research section, and it's still under review.
It's about Infoblox D D I, meaning D N S, DHCP and IP address management, on Infoblox's NIOS Grid and its cloud-managed service, Universal D D I.
It's for the architects and engineers deciding whether to build an agency's name and address layer on Infoblox, and how to run it if they do.
After a short orientation, Part 1 covers the platform and the case for it, including fed-ramp scope, the competition and the risks.
Part 2 covers how a central team hands D D I to divisions without losing control.
Every fact comes from a primary source opened on October twenty-second, 2026, and marketing is called a vendor claim.
2: Almost every connection an agency makes starts with a D N S lookup, and in a hybrid, multi-cloud estate that answer decides far more than an address.
DHCP and address management sit right beside it, because lease history is how an address maps to a device, and the address plan is the record behind the inventory directives.
So this deck treats all three as one control plane.
Book 08 of the workbook describes that plane: on-premises servers that answer, a management plane that holds the system of record, and local resolvers that keep working if it's unreachable.
The argument of the session is simple.
The rules need one governed D D I plane, and Infoblox is one of the strongest ways to build it, with real risks to manage.
3: Here's what the rules actually require, stated as capabilities.
Sign agency zones and validate answers, with the 2008 DNSSEC memo still in force.
Use encrypted D N S wherever it's technically supported, and forward to sis-uh's Protective D N S upstream.

Logging is subtle: the May 2026 memo that replaced the old logging memo doesn't mention D N S at all, so D N S and DHCP logging is carried forward by sis-uh's Logging Reference Architecture, with six months searchable and twelve retrievable.
And the inventory directives want regular discovery of agency address space and attestation of public addresses and domains.
No rule names Infoblox or any D D I vendor, so choosing a platform is an architecture decision.
4: The names have changed and a lot of older material is now wrong, so we'll get an accurate picture: the Grid, the cloud side and its limits, D N S, DHCP and eye-pam, security, automation and logging.
5: The NIOS Grid is a group of appliances sharing one distributed database, run from a single point, the Grid Master, which every administrator goes through.
Members can be physical hardware or virtual appliances, singly or in high-availability pairs, and they talk to the Grid Master over encrypted tunnels.
A Grid Master Candidate holds a full copy, but promoting it is a manual job you can't do from the cloud portal.
The current hardware is Trinzic X6, and the virtual appliances run on VMware and every major cloud, with Azure Government explicitly covered.
On versions, NIOS 9.1.0 went GA in March 2026, and 9.0.6 started a long-term-support train.
6: Universal D D I is the cloud-managed side, renamed from BloxOne D D I in September 2024, and run from what's now called the Infoblox Portal.

Its servers run either on your infrastructure or as a service from Infoblox's points of presence, and its management plane reaches out to the major cloud D N S services and to Microsoft D N S and DHCP.
Infoblox markets it as a single control plane; that's a vendor claim, and Infoblox's own pages show why you should test it.
The Portal can't promote a Grid Master Candidate or manage DHCP failover, the as-a-service option has no IPv6, and the cloud D N S sync handles only simple records.
So "one console" is overstated: in practice you'll run both consoles side by side.
7: D N S on NIOS is strong, with a catch for each feature.

D N S views give different answers to different clients, and that's how you'd point internal traffic at sis-uh's Protective D N S. DNSSEC signing is central, done only by the Grid Master as a hidden primary, with keys there or on an external hardware security module, and automatic key rollovers.

D N S Firewall blocks bad names with response policy zones, the Grid can manage Windows D N S and DHCP servers without an agent, and from 9.1, encrypted D N S is served, but only on X6 appliances, free there and an extra license on X5.
And one setting you must change: the default signing algorithm is RSA with SHA-1, so pick something stronger before you sign.
8: Failover peers talk to each other directly; the Grid Master isn't involved, whatever older material says.
But failover is IPv4 only, which matters under the IPv6 mandate, though Windows has the same gap.
Lease history is archived, which is the address-to-asset record nist asks for.

On the eye-pam side, a network view is a single routing domain, and discovery tools read both the network and the clouds, though the deeper device discovery needs its own license and dedicated appliances, so budget for that.
Two corrections to common claims: separate network views permit overlap, they don't prevent it.
And the AWS address-management integration excludes GovCloud.
9: Infoblox Threat Defense is the D N S-layer security product.
It blocks bad names, shares threat intelligence, and detects things like D N S tunneling, data exfiltration and command-and-control.
It runs from the cloud or on premises, and one detection mode streams D N S metadata, including client addresses, to the cloud, so treat that as a boundary decision, not a checkbox.
Licensing comes in four tiers, with the cloud pieces in the upper two.
There's one strong independent signal: Google Cloud's own documentation describes its D N S Armor threat detection as powered by Infoblox.
Then there are the marketing figures about how many threats it stops and how early.
Nobody independent has verified them, so keep them out of anything an assessor reads.
10: Automation and logging decide whether the platform can be governed at scale.
On automation, Infoblox is ahead of the other D D I vendors.

NIOS has a REST API with modern sign-in from 9.1, and the Terraform provider moved to a 3.0 beta on October thirteenth that covers both NIOS and Universal D D I but isn't backward compatible, so plan that migration.
Ansible and ServiceNow integrations exist too.
Full query logging adds load, the dnstap stream drops logs if its receiver is down, and the built-in reporting appliances lock after repeated overruns of their daily ingest caps.
So for federal retention, send logs to the sim and size reporting deliberately.
11: Module 2 is the case for Infoblox.

We'll map each federal requirement to an Infoblox feature, read exactly what the fed-ramp listing covers, compare the competition, and lay out the risks, because a recommendation that hides its risks isn't usable.
12: This is the core of the argument: each requirement, the Infoblox feature that delivers it, and what to watch.
Signing and resilient D N S map to the Grid Master and Grid replication, but candidate promotion is manual, so it belongs in a tested runbook.
Encrypted D N S works on X6 hardware only.
Protective D N S forwarding works per view, but no Infoblox document was found on encrypted forwarding to sis-uh, so confirm it in a lab.
Logging and inventory are well covered, with the caps and hardware we just saw.
IPv6 is there, but without DHCP failover.
And validated cryptography is the real gap, with no active certificate today.
Still, seven of eight requirements land on one platform and one database.
13: fed-ramp is the most misquoted part of any Infoblox proposal, so let's read the record.
The Marketplace lists Infoblox Government Cloud as fed-ramp Certified at Moderate, as SaaS in AWS GovCloud, with one agency authorization and a reuse count of zero.
It covers Universal D D I and some security services, but not everything; ask Infoblox for the authorization boundary diagram.
And the biggest point: NIOS appliances and virtual appliances on agency infrastructure aren't a cloud service, so no fed-ramp authorization covers them.
They sit inside the agency's own boundary, and that's the path for High or DoD systems.
With reuse at zero, expect to do your own ATO work.
Ask, too, for a list of features the fed-ramp instance has versus commercial.
14: A narrower question: if an agency buys Trinzic, the physical appliances, how well does the hardware fit Book 08's design?
The Grid gives one shared database with an HA Grid Master and a candidate, though promotion is manual and Infoblox publishes no scale limits, so size it with the vendor.
Domain controllers can send Kerberos-signed updates to it, signing is central, and eye-pam is built in.
The watch points are the ones we've seen: change the signing default, X6 for free encrypted D N S, dedicated appliances for deep discovery, and reporting caps.
Trinzic sits inside the agency's boundary, outside the fed-ramp listing.
And its FIPS 140-2 certificate went historical in September, with newer modules pending.
15: Can Trinzic run an agency's D D I alone once workloads move to the clouds?
On its own, it can see into them, discovering networks and importing zones one way, but it can't own cloud D N S.

There are three ways to extend it, and they combine: virtual appliances in each cloud, Universal D D I, which is the only Infoblox path that writes back to cloud D N S, or native cloud resolvers wired to the Grid with forwarding both ways.

The design guidance is this: mostly on premises, use native resolvers with forwarding; hybrid, add virtual appliances; multi-cloud at Moderate, add Universal D D I; in GovCloud or Azure Government at Moderate, confirm the government edition supports those accounts first; and for fed-ramp High or the higher Defense levels, don't depend on the Moderate SaaS.
The Trinzic explainer has the full reasoning.
16: Now the assurance evidence, checked on October twenty-second.
There's no C I S Benchmark for NIOS, so the hardening baseline is the agency's own settings, drawn from nist's D N S guide and Infoblox's documentation.
Infoblox does have two current DISA STIGs, which neither BlueCat nor EfficientIP has; they're High only, Defense material, but useful cross-checks.
FIPS 140 is the weak spot, so let's say it plainly.
Infoblox has no active certificate today.
Its FIPS 140-2 certificates moved to the historical list with the September 21, 2026 sunset, and four FIPS 140-3 submissions are still in nist's queue.
There's no current NIAP certificate either, with NIOS 9.0 in evaluation.

And a note on nist's D N S deployment guide: it's the best practical guide we have, but two of its three authors are Infoblox employees, so disclose that whenever you cite it in support of choosing Infoblox.
17: On fed-ramp, Infoblox is the only dedicated D D I vendor with a listing, though the hyperscalers' government clouds sit at High, a higher ceiling.
On FIPS 140, BlueCat leads with an active FIPS 140-3 certificate valid to 2029.
Infoblox is the only one with its own STIGs, a High only reference, and has the broadest D N S security set.
On automation, it has the deepest.
DHCPv6 failover is missing everywhere we checked, so it's no differentiator.
And alternatives do win in places: BlueCat's Micetro manages existing Windows and BIND servers in place, and a single-cloud workload may need no third-party plane at all.
So the fair claim is a strong default for a hybrid federal estate, not the only viable choice.
18: Now the risks, stated plainly, with how to manage each.
First, cryptographic validation: no active FIPS certificate today.
If your system needs validated cryptography at award, tie go-live to the issued certificate, or carry the gap as a dated POA&M item, and ask which NIOS versions the pending modules cover.
Second, no current NIAP certificate, and the CDM product list is closed, so don't promise anyone that status.
Third, vulnerabilities: NIOS has had CVEs rated as high as 9.8, though none is in sis-uh's known exploited catalog, so write the patch cadence into the ATO plan.
Fourth, NIOS runs on BIND, so ask for a BIND advisory commitment.
And fifth, the SaaS tops out at Moderate with zero reuse.
19: The second set of risks is about cost, capacity and features.
Universal D D I licensing uses subscription tokens that expire at the end of the term, so model total cost over three to five years, including a hardware refresh.
Size the reporting tier for the retention you need, or make the sim the system of record.
Plan the hardware refresh around encrypted D N S, put a stronger signing algorithm in the build standard, and keep Grid Manager runbooks for what the Portal can't do.
Ignore stale collateral and cite only the Marketplace record.
Then turn the risks into contract obligations: a certificate timeline with a remedy if it slips, a BIND advisory commitment, the fed-ramp boundary diagram, and a data export guarantee.
20: Part 2 is about divisions under central governance, starting with NIOS.
Most agencies aren't one network, and a central plane only works if divisions can still do their jobs through it, because a division that can't will work around it.
21: The NIOS permission model starts from the right place: everything is denied by default, so a new group sees nothing until you grant it something.
Permissions can cover every object of a type, or one specific object and what's inside it, and they inherit downward, with more specific settings overriding.
When permissions overlap, the first match wins.
So if one role grants read-only and a later role grants read-write on the same records, the admin gets read-only, which can surprise you.
Be careful with the built-in D N S and DHCP admin roles, which are far too broad for a division.
And the governance lever: only superusers create groups and roles, so a division can't widen its own rights.
22: Here's the recipe for scoping one admin group to one division.
Create a limited-access group with only the interfaces it needs; help-desk staff can be restricted to running approved tasks.
Grant read-write on the division's own address space and its own zones, with read-only on the parent view, and confine its service work to its own servers.
Leave everything else at the default deny.
Then the step people miss: turn on the Grid setting that makes address records need rights on both the zone and the address block.
Without it, a division with write access to a shared zone could point a name at another division's addresses.
That one setting is what keeps divisions honest.
Next, the constructs that separate them.
23: Three constructs separate divisions on NIOS, and each has a rule that shapes the design.

Network views let two divisions hold the same addresses, but a DHCP server serves only one view, so a division with overlapping space needs its own DHCP servers, and nothing on NIOS enforces uniqueness across views.
D N S views give different answers to different clients, and the first match wins, so a catch-all external view placed first hides the internal one.
And extensible attributes tag objects with things like Division or cost center.
Two cautions: a required tag can be skipped through the API, so automation must enforce it, and tags drive reports, not permissions.
Access is always scoped by objects.
24: The approval workflow is how central keeps a hand on division changes without doing the work.
A division submits, a central group approves, reschedules or rejects, and approved tasks run with the submitter's own permissions and land in the audit log.
The riskiest operations, like signing zones, rolling keys, or resizing networks, are blocked for submitters entirely, which suits a federal model well.
Infoblox's own page says CSV imports do not require approvals.
Leave that permission in place and a division can load a thousand records with no review at all.
So remove CSV import from every division group, and give bulk loads to a central group under a change ticket.
25: Who can sign in, and which group they land in, is the other half of division scoping.
NIOS maps directory groups to its own admin groups, with the first match winning, so an A D group per division can decide where an administrator belongs.
For federal staff, the important path is certificate sign-in with CAC or piv, checked against OCSP.
sam-ul works too, including with Entra, where the user lands in the group whose name exactly matches.

A few things to test: certificate sign-in to the API can conflict with certain cloud licenses, sam-ul-only users get no command line, and it's not confirmed whether Entra sends the group name or its ID.
Order mappings carefully, and keep a local break-glass admin.
26: Three topics close the NIOS module.
First, a division still running Windows D N S and DHCP can be managed from the Grid, with the division's group given rights on its own servers only, not the system-wide Microsoft roles.
Second, what stays central in every design: the Grid Master, DNSSEC keys and signing, security policy, the definitions of groups and roles, sign-in policy, and the top-level address blocks.
Third, a limitation that surprises almost everyone.
NIOS reporting doesn't filter by permissions, so a division with the reporting app sees agency-wide D N S and DHCP data.
That matters a great deal for a law-enforcement bureau.
So scope reporting by sharing dashboards per division instead.
27: Divisions aren't the only way to cut D D I.
Many agencies split it by service, with D N S, DHCP and eye-pam teams working across the whole agency, and NIOS supports that with the same model.
This is an illustrative design, not a validated configuration.
The D N S team gets its views, zones and D N S servers, with no network rights.
The DHCP team is where the catch is: a permission on a network also covers its ranges, so grant the ranges and fixed addresses directly instead.
The eye-pam team gets the address containers, with an explicit deny on DHCP ranges if that team owns them.
And the same Grid-wide setting from before becomes a deliberate check between the D N S and eye-pam teams.
28: Service teams and divisions aren't alternatives; most agencies combine them, because a grant can be scoped by service and by address space at once.

The central D N S team keeps the agency's top zone and DNSSEC signing, the central eye-pam team keeps the top-level blocks and hands each division its own, and divisions take over DHCP inside their own space.
On Universal D D I the picture changes, and there's a documentation conflict over whether separate D N S and DHCP roles are supported in this release, so confirm with Infoblox.
And one caution applies however you split: on NIOS, reports ignore permissions, so anyone with the reporting app sees agency-wide data.
29: Module 4 covers divisions on Universal D D I, and the operating model.
We'll look at its access views and eye-pam Federation, then four delegation patterns, a worked example, who does what, and a rollout sequence.
30: On Universal D D I, the division construct is the access view, a container for a division's D D I resources.
Corporate admins create one level of sub-views, and divisional admins can't see anything outside theirs.
Assign an IP space and everything in it follows.
The constraints are significant: users and roles are defined only centrally, access views can't be renamed or deleted, so name them carefully, and service users with API keys can't log in to one.
The big gain over NIOS is eye-pam Federation, which enforces address uniqueness across Universal D D I, NIOS and cloud eye-pam, including deliberate overlap behind NAT.
And remember the documentation conflict on supported roles.
31: Put together, these give four delegation patterns, and most agencies mix them.
Pattern A is one central Grid with scoped admin groups and approvals, the default, with risks like permission sprawl and the import bypass.
Pattern B gives a division its own servers inside the Grid, for local resilience, while signed zones still keep a central primary.
Pattern C gives a division its own network view or IP space, the only way to hold overlapping address space.
And pattern D delegates a zone to servers the division runs itself: full autonomy, but central loses the audit trail, security policy coverage and signing for that zone.
Use A by default, B for resilience, C only for overlap, and D only where autonomy is worth it.
32: Here's an illustrative design, not a validated configuration, for an agency with four divisions.
Headquarters is the central operations team.
A law-enforcement bureau needs confidentiality, so it gets its own servers, pattern B.
A regional office still runs Windows D N S and DHCP, managed from the Grid with rights on those servers only.
And a research lab whose range overlaps headquarters gets its own network view and DHCP servers, pattern C, with its zone delegated to its own servers, pattern D.

Across the Grid: object permissions turned on, so headquarters can't point a name into the bureau's space, no CSV import for any division, one approval workflow each, and the bureau's data kept out of shared dashboards.
33: This matrix is adapted from Book 08's, which separates deciding from doing, with a column added for divisions.
The C I O decides the platform and how divisions are scoped, and the central D D I team builds it, with divisions consulted, because a scope they can't work in becomes a workaround.
The authorizing official decides whether a cloud management plane is authorized.
The see-so decides the control requirements, like signing and security policy, and central D D I runs them.
Standard record changes are where delegation pays off: central defines them in advance, and divisions do the work.
And an encrypted D N S exception with no end date goes to the authorizing official.
34: To close, the rollout follows Book 08's order, adapted for divisions: inventory everything first, build the central pieces, coexist with the Windows servers in place, onboard divisions one at a time starting with pattern A, federate the clouds, then harden and evidence.

The decisions to take now are the platform model for each impact level, the delegation pattern per division, whether to wait for the FIPS certificate or proceed with a POA&M, and where logs will live.
Then send Infoblox the procurement asks and lab-test the open questions.
In the program's analysis, Infoblox is one of the strongest ways to build a governed D D I plane, as long as you manage its risks in the open.
This is research under review, not an endorsement by any federal agency.
